newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar's nosedive chokes dual-currency bond boom.
newsitem.headline: Dollar's nosedive chokes dual-currency bond boom.

text.p: The dollar's nosedive against the yen has choked a boom in yen-based dual currency bond issues by generating tremendous foreign exchange losses for underwriting brokers, industry sources said.
The dollar has taken a more than 15 yen nosedive against the yen since early May and fell to as low as 111.98 yen in late trading on Tuesday.
Many brokerages are exposed to heavy currency losses on dual-currency bonds with currency options, as they have trouble selling them to investors after the recent dollar dive.

Such options-linked bonds enable bond holders to receive high coupons in yen at maturity, usually about three to six months, if foreign exchange rates stay above levels agreed at the time of the launch, but they have to take heavy losses if they break below that level.
Underwriting sources said a total of about 200 billion yen worth of options-linked bonds had been offered, especially by smaller and mid-sized brokerages, in recent months.
Unless such bonds are sold to investors, underwriting brokers have to take currency losses themselves.

On Friday, Ichiyoshi Securities Co Ltd said it would accept the cancellation of contracts by individual investors who committed to buy 5.1 percent such forex-linked dual-currency bonds issued by Norway's Eksportfinans.
Ichiyoshi said the yen value of the bonds fell sharply after the dollar slid below the knock out price of 115.80 yen.
"We decided to accept the cancellations by investors after the dollar dropped below the knock out level of 115.80 yen during the subscription period," the official said.

"Some brokerages have managed to sell those bonds at a heavy discount to investors, but many of them are still holding on to them, waiting for the dollar to recover again," an underwriter at medium-sized Japanese securities firm said.
"This can be a fatal blow to some brokerages with weak capital bases and the problem will not be solved unless the dollar rises again convincingly," he said.
Dual-currency issues left over in the market can have an enormous negative impact on smaller brokerages, as they eat up much of brokers' profits, a senior Japanese banker said.
Amid sluggish demand for stocks in the past few years, many securities firms have depended heavily on revenues from underwriting foreign bonds, especially dual currency issues.
As the dollar tumbled, brokerages had to cancel sales or accept cancellation of sales of such bonds as the value of the dual-currency bonds was deeply eroded in yen terms.

"Many of those bonds had set up an options level when the dollar was standing above 125-126 yen, so many of the knockout levels were set at between 117 to 119 yen. Looking how the dollar is diving now investors must be suffering heavy losses," an senior underwriting source said.

Investors were encouraged to buy dual-currency bonds by the uptrend of the dollar over the past two years and brokerages fed these to them aggressively without giving much consideration to currency risks as the greenback had been climbing so consistently, the industry sources said.

"We may have to reconsider our strategy. Many brokerages have been depending heavily on debt-based instrument offerings, especially dual-currency bonds," said a senior manager of the international finance section at a major Japanese brokerage.
"We may have to look for other alternatives and may especially have to avoid offering instruments which contain currency risks," the manager said.
